author: Yellowstone Times
title: Montana State University marks first year milestone for new midwifery doctorate
text:
Waded Cruzado President of Montana State University | Montana State University
Waded Cruzado President of Montana State University | Montana State University
Montana State University’s Mark and Robyn Jones College of Nursing has completed the first year of its Doctor of Nursing Practice nurse-midwifery program, the first such program in Montana. The program, which began in fall 2024, was established to address the shortage of nurse-midwives in the state and improve maternal and infant health outcomes.
Mariah Hill, who leads the program, noted that before its launch, Montanans interested in becoming nurse-midwives had to leave the state or pursue distance learning from out-of-state institutions. This lack of local options contributed to workforce shortages in a state where more than half of counties do not have a women’s health specialist and where maternal and infant mortality rates are higher than national averages.
“This is a key step towards transforming maternal and infant health outcomes in Montana,” Hill said. “It’s been incredible seeing the widespread support there is for this program, and people who are not midwives saying what we need are more nurse-midwives in Montana.”
The three-year DNP program admitted its first cohort of seven students last year; they are expected to graduate in spring 2027. A new group of six students will begin this fall, with a part-time four-year option also available. The college already offers DNP degrees for psychiatric mental health nurse practitioners and family nurse practitioners.
Graduates must pass a National Board Exam to become certified nurse-midwives. These professionals can prescribe medication, provide primary care throughout a woman’s life starting from adolescence, and work both in hospitals and community-based settings. Currently, about four dozen nurse-midwives practice in Montana, mostly concentrated in urban areas.
To design the curriculum, MSU worked with experienced nurse-midwives from across Montana and beyond beginning in 2022. The degree is delivered online asynchronously to accommodate students across rural and tribal communities. Clinical training includes two intensive skills weeks on campus in Bozeman as well as at least 765 clinical hours with practicing nurse-midwives.
“Our students are all over Montana, with many living in rural and tribal communities. It is really worth the extra challenge of figuring out how to accommodate students living in Montana’s most isolated communities to be able to build a maternal health workforce where we need it most,” Hill said. “I know at the end of the day how important it is to provide a program that meets students where they're at, and where they can keep being part of their families and communities.”
Honey Newton, an instructor for the program who also runs Heart and Hands Midwifery and Family Healthcare in Kalispell, said common barriers include travel distances for classes or clinicals, finding placements amid workforce shortages, education costs, loss of income from leaving jobs, moving families, or other disruptions.
“I think all of those factors are barriers that MSU is addressing well with their new nurse-midwifery program,” Newton said. “MSU should be very proud that they put this together and are pulling it off.”
Newton added that recruiting students who intend to stay local supports building capacity for women’s healthcare across rural areas.
Student Mariah Holdbrook from Roberts said she was motivated by learning about high maternal mortality rates within Montana compared to other states—a persistent issue according to recent data—and wants her future work as a mobile women’s health provider to reach underserved populations.
Of her experience so far she said remote learning works well given her prior asynchronous studies but acknowledged some isolation due to limited face-to-face interaction with peers. She noted balancing family life would make attending an on-campus program difficult or impossible for herself or others.
Hill emphasized that expanding access goes beyond birth attendance: “We wear a lot of hats,” she said. “Having more nurse-midwives in more Montana counties will mean more than just attending births. Our graduates are going to increase women's access to basic primary care and reproductive health services.”
Students take courses covering pharmacology; primary care; gynecological care; pregnancy; birth; postpartum; newborn care; among others.
Funding for the initiative comes from Mark and Robyn Jones’ $101 million donation made to MSU in 2021—one of the largest gifts ever received by a nursing college nationwide—and $3 million from Intermountain St. Vincent Regional Hospital specifically earmarked for endowing this midwifery program.
Hill thanked early participants: “We want our students to have a really excellent, high quality educational experience,” she said. “We really welcome student feedback, and it will play a huge role in helping us make the program even better for future students."
Sarah Shannon, dean of the College of Nursing often says: “Montana is a great place to raise a family,” adding: “We want to help ensure it is also a great place to start a family.”
